title: Psychologist
protagonist: Harriet Gluberton, founder of the Academy For Courtroom Reporters (AFCR)
primary_metric: each finalist slate's composite score -- the equal-weighted mean of its three admitted applicants' five normalized (0-100) category scores

options.A: Admit The Standout Slate -- the three applicants (Sophia, Spencer, Riley) with AFCR's highest single best-category normalized score
options.B: Admit The Balanced Slate -- the three applicants (Sophia, Tyler, Brigitte) with AFCR's highest composite (all-category average) normalized score

new_coverage_note: This is a legacy-conversion case, not a newly-authored one. Every one of the 7 claimed standards already has n>0 in standards_spine.json (measurement-ratio, advanced-numbers-percent, advanced-numbers-how-to-convert-numbers-to-percents, statistics-and-probability-mean, statistics-and-probability-how-to-find-the-mean-of-a-set-of-data, number-sense-how-to-compare-two-or-more-values, number-sense-bar-graph), so new_coverage[] is genuinely empty -- not padded. The spine was searched for any n==0 skill plausibly related to normalization, weighted averages, composite scores, percentile, or z-scores (there is no z-score/standard-deviation/percentile skill in the spine at all) and none exists that this case's actual deliverables force. See legacy_conversion_note.
legacy_conversion_note: Converted from source/Y3/Additional/Psychologist/Case Study_ Psychology.docx and Guides Notes.docx per cases/_concepts/LEGACY_DILEMMA_LOCKS_2026-08-20.md's 'psychologist' entry. The ORIGINAL dilemma in the source was an open 'pick 3 of 27 applicants' selection problem with no named binary fork. The only concrete binary fork present anywhere in the source materials was the Guide Notes' 'Twist': converting AFCR to a single-gender (girls-only or boys-only) admissions school, framed around which gender 'produces better court reporters.' That framing is discriminatory and has been discarded entirely -- it is not used, referenced, or alluded to anywhere in this conversion (not in case.md, not in FACILITATOR.md, not as a contrast). Gender is not a data column in the source spreadsheet and does not appear anywhere in this case. The locked replacement binary (single-best-score vs. composite-score admission, per the lock file) is a genuine, unrelated ranking-methodology tension built fresh from the applicant pool's real multi-dimension test data (4 short-term memory tests + typing speed per applicant, source/Y3/Additional/Psychologist/Case Study_ Psychology.xlsx) -- verified during conversion that this framing is cleanly supported: normalizing each of the 27 applicants' 5 raw scores to a percent of the pool's best score in that category and ranking by single-best vs. composite average produces two real, different top-3 lists (2 of 3 seats differ) with a defensible <20% margin either direction. Age is present in the source data (and reproduced in Appendix B for completeness) but is explicitly excluded from both admission rules (Appendix C, MA3) -- neither the discarded gender axis nor an age axis plays any role in this case's math.

sources.claim: NCRA Registered Professional Reporter (RPR) skills-exam speed requirement, top leg (Testimony/Q&A)
sources.title: RPR Certification Requirements and Exam Structure
sources.note: Secondary source (legal-info publisher) describing NCRA's own three-leg RPR skills exam (Literary 180 WPM, Jury Charge 200 WPM, Testimony/Q&A 225 WPM, each at 95%+ accuracy). Used only as scene-setting texture in Background establishing the profession's real speed bar -- not load-bearing to any calculation in this case.

sources.claim: Equal ('unit') weighting is the standard default method for combining multiple scores into a composite score, absent a validated/empirically-derived weighting scheme
sources.title: Composite Scores (section 13.4.1, Calculating a Weighted Composite Score)
sources.note: Educational-methodology source, no listed author or publication date. Grade MEDIUM (soft on 'dated'), used to back Appendix C's Modeling Assumption MA2 (equal weighting of the five categories). Corrected 2026-08-20 after a data-decay check: the source states equal-weighted composites are 'the most common kind of composite score' in clinical practice -- it does not use language like 'simplest/most transparent' or 'neutral default'; that normative framing was the case author's own judgment (MA2's own text), not a claim from this source. case.md and this note now attribute only the 'most common practice' fact to the source.

modeling_assumptions.text: Normalization basis: every raw score is converted to a percent of the highest raw score any applicant in this year's pool achieved in that category (not a fixed external maximum), because none of the five categories has a public, universally agreed ceiling. Load-bearing -- see case.md Appendix C for the full statement; the sensitivity direction/magnitude is facilitator-only (see FACILITATOR.md).

Weighting: the five categories are weighted equally (1/5 each) in the composite score, per the standard default in composite-scoring methodology absent a validated alternative weighting [S2]. Load-bearing -- flexing this is exactly what Tier 2 probe 5 and the case's own Twist do; see FACILITATOR.md.

Age (reproduced in Appendix B because AFCR collects it) is excluded from both ranking methods. Not load-bearing to either computed ranking -- included as deliberately irrelevant appendix data per SPEC's T3+ filtering-practice guidance, and as an explicit anti-discriminatory scope statement: this case's math never selects on age (or on any characteristic other than the five measured test categories).
Rounding: normalized scores and composite scores round to one decimal place throughout.

deliverables.text: A normalized-score table for all 27 applicants: each of the five measured categories converted to a percent of the highest raw score achieved in that category, shown alongside the raw scores.
For every applicant: their single-best normalized score (max of the five category percentages) and their composite score (mean of the five category percentages), to one decimal place.
Two ranked top-3 admit lists -- one by single-best normalized score, one by composite score -- with every applicant's rank number shown.
One original bar graph comparing The Standout Slate's and The Balanced Slate's three admits on whichever normalized metric the pitch argues matters most.

balance.argument_a: On the case's own composite metric, The Standout Slate (Sophia, Spencer, Riley) still averages a strong 72.3 -- and on the metric its own selection rule directly optimizes (average single-best normalized score), it posts a perfect 100.0 across all three admits: each of the three leads AFCR's entire applicant pool outright in at least one of the five measured categories (Sophia in three categories, Spencer and Riley one each). No applicant on The Balanced Slate leads the pool in any single category outright.
balance.argument_b: On the case's stated primary metric -- composite score, the equal-weighted mean across all five normalized categories -- The Balanced Slate (Sophia, Tyler, Brigitte) averages 79.0 against The Standout Slate's 72.3, a real and defensible edge. Two of The Balanced Slate's three admits (Tyler, Brigitte) never post the single highest score in any one category, but neither do they have a weak category the way Standout's Spencer (33.3 in Test 3) or Riley (46.7 in Test 2) do.
balance.margin_basis: Primary metric (composite score, case.json.primary_metric): The Balanced Slate leads by 9.3%, well inside SPEC's 20% cap. The reverse lens -- average single-best normalized score, the metric The Standout Slate's own rule optimizes -- favors The Standout Slate; see case.json.derived for the exact figure, kept out of case.md and this argument text per case-write's no-leaked-result rule.

derived._note: Worked from Appendix B's given applicant data using Appendix C's stated normalization (MA1, percent of pool max per category) and equal weighting (MA2). Computed during conversion; case-readiness should re-derive independently via sensitivity_model.py, not just trust this block.
derived.twist_note: Post-twist, both rosters share 2 of 3 names (Riley and Tyler) -- the entire disagreement collapses to one seat: Spencer (Standout Slate's pick) vs. Brigitte (Balanced Slate's pick).

sensitivity_note: The composite-vs-single-best margin (9.3%) is sensitive to two stated modeling choices: the normalization basis (MA1) and the category weighting (MA2). See FACILITATOR.md and sensitivity_model.py -- flexing MA2's typing weight does not flip which slate wins the composite metric, but does narrow the margin materially.
